subject: Economics
description: Articles, Annual Financial Statement, types of expenditure, FRBM, recent reforms

questions.stem: The Indian Union Budget — formally the 'Annual Financial Statement' — is provided for under:

options.option_text: Article 110
Article 112
Article 280
Article 246

questions.explanation: Article 112 — President shall cause the AFS (estimated receipts + expenditure) of the Government of India for a financial year to be laid before both Houses of Parliament. Article 110 — Money Bill definition. Article 280 — Finance Commission. Article 246 — distribution of legislative powers (lists). The Finance Bill (taxation proposals) and Appropriation Bill (withdrawal authorisation) are presented alongside.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The Union Budget is currently presented on:

options.option_text: Last working day of February (old tradition)
1 February (advanced from end of February since 2017)
31 March
1 April

questions.explanation: Earlier the Budget was presented on the last working day of February at 5 PM (British colonial timing). Yashwant Sinha (NDA-1) advanced timing to 11 AM IST in 1999. Arun Jaitley (Modi govt) advanced the date to 1 February starting Budget 2017-18 — to enable expenditure to start from 1 April (start of FY) without 'vote on account'. The Railway Budget (separate since 1924, Acworth Committee) was MERGED with Union Budget from 2017-18.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: FRBM Act, 2003 (Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act) was enacted to:

options.option_text: Establish RBI as central bank
Reduce fiscal deficit and ensure inter-generational equity in fiscal management
Levy income tax
Create the GST Council

questions.explanation: FRBM Act 2003 — set targets to cap fiscal deficit (3% of GDP) and revenue deficit (zero) by 2008-09 (later extended). Mandates Medium-Term Fiscal Policy Statement, FRBM compliance reports. N.K. Singh Committee (2017) recommended replacement with FRBM 2.0 — flexible glide path with 'escape clauses' for emergencies. Fiscal deficit hit ~9.2% of GDP during COVID (FY 2020-21). Current target — 4.4% (FY 2025-26), 4.3% (FY 2026-27); aiming toward 3% by FY 2028-29.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: Total Government expenditure consists of two main categories:

options.option_text: Central + State expenditure
Revenue Expenditure (recurring) + Capital Expenditure (asset creation)
Defence + Civilian
Direct + Indirect spending

questions.explanation: Two-fold classification. REVENUE EXPENDITURE — recurring, doesn't create asset (salaries, pensions, interest payments, subsidies, defence revenue, grants to states). Largest share — typically 75-80%. CAPITAL EXPENDITURE — asset-creating (infrastructure, defence equipment, capital outlay on PSUs, loans to states). Around 20-25%. Government has been emphasising capex — FY 2025-26 capex budget ~₹11.1 lakh crore. Plan vs Non-Plan distinction was abolished in 2017 — only Revenue/Capital classification remains.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: FISCAL DEFICIT is best defined as:

options.option_text: Government revenue minus government expenditure
Total expenditure − Total receipts (excluding borrowings); essentially the borrowing requirement
Trade deficit
Capital receipts only

questions.explanation: Fiscal Deficit (FD) = Total Expenditure − (Total Receipts excluding borrowings) = Total Borrowings of the Government. This is what gets 'financed' by issuing G-Secs, raising loans, drawing down cash balance. Other deficit measures: Revenue Deficit (Revenue Expenditure − Revenue Receipts); Primary Deficit (FD − Interest Payments); Effective Revenue Deficit (Revenue Deficit − Grants for capital asset creation, abandoned 2022). India aims for fiscal deficit < 4.5% by FY 2025-26 per FRBM trajectory.

questions.stem: The 'Vote on Account' permits the government to:

options.option_text: Levy new taxes for the next 6 months
Withdraw money from the Consolidated Fund of India for a part of the year (typically 2 months) before full Budget approval
Sign foreign treaties
Transfer state taxes

questions.explanation: Vote on Account (Article 116) — interim authorisation for Government to draw from CFI (typically for 2 months — covers election period before a new government's full budget). Used in election years OR if budget is delayed. NO new taxation can be introduced. The full Annual Budget is presented later by the new government. Distinct from 'Interim Budget' which is the practice of an outgoing government presenting a brief budget before elections — typically a Vote on Account + minor tax tweaks.

questions.stem: Largest source of CENTRAL government's tax revenue (FY 2024-25) is:

options.option_text: Customs Duty
GST + Income tax combined dominate (Income Tax slightly larger than GST)
Wealth Tax
Property Tax

questions.explanation: Top tax sources (FY 24-25): Income Tax (incl. corporate ~30%, personal ~25-28% of gross tax), GST (~26-28%), Customs (~7%), Excise on petroleum (~6%), Cesses/Surcharges. Personal income tax has overtaken corporate tax in recent years. Direct tax (income, corporate) ≈ 55-58% of total; indirect (GST, customs) ≈ 42-45%. Composition has shifted toward direct taxes post-GST. Non-tax revenue (RBI dividend, PSU dividends, fees) is also substantial — RBI alone gave ~₹2.1 lakh crore in 2024.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The Contingency Fund of India, established under Article 267 of the Constitution, is held in the custody of whom?

options.option_text: The Speaker of Lok Sabha, on behalf of Parliament
The President of India, on behalf of the Union
The Finance Minister, as head of Union finances
The Reserve Bank of India, as banker to the government

questions.explanation: Article 267(1) vests custody of the Contingency Fund of India in the President, who may advance money from it for urgent unforeseen expenditure pending parliamentary authorisation. The Finance Minister manages the budget process but does not hold this fund; the RBI acts as the government's banker but has no constitutional custodial role over the Contingency Fund.

questions.stem: The Economic Survey, released on the eve of the Union Budget, is prepared under the guidance of which authority?

options.option_text: NITI Aayog, under the Vice Chairperson's supervision
Ministry of Finance's Department of Economic Affairs
Reserve Bank of India's Monetary Policy Department
Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation

questions.explanation: The Economic Survey is prepared by the Economic Division of the Department of Economic Affairs (DEA), Ministry of Finance, under the Chief Economic Adviser (CEA). It is tabled in Parliament before Budget Day. NITI Aayog prepares policy documents and strategy papers but not the Economic Survey; MoSPI publishes GDP and other statistical data separately.

questions.stem: Rajya Sabha cannot enforce amendments to an Appropriation Bill — it can only return recommendations which Lok Sabha may reject. The constitutional root of this arrangement lies in:

options.option_text: Article 109, which defines the parliamentary procedure applicable to Money Bills
Article 110, which classifies Appropriation Bills as a category of Money Bills
Article 117, which restricts introduction of all financial bills to Lok Sabha
Article 112, which designates the Annual Financial Statement as a Money Bill

questions.explanation: Article 110(1)(d) expressly classifies a bill providing for appropriation of moneys out of the Consolidated Fund of India as a Money Bill. Once classified as a Money Bill, the procedure in Article 109 follows — Rajya Sabha may only recommend amendments. Article 109 is the procedural consequence, not the root cause. Article 117 covers financial bills that are not Money Bills; Article 112 deals with the Annual Financial Statement, not classification of bills.

questions.stem: Zero-Based Budgeting (ZBB), adopted by India in 1983 for Plan schemes, differs from traditional incremental budgeting primarily because it requires:

options.option_text: Every scheme to justify its full expenditure from scratch each year
Budget allocations to be linked to GDP growth projections for the year
A mandatory 10% reduction in non-essential expenditure every year
Parliament to approve only the incremental increase over the prior year

questions.explanation: Under ZBB, each budget cycle begins at zero — every programme must justify its entire resource requirement afresh, regardless of past allocations. Traditional incremental budgeting merely adjusts the previous year's figures. ZBB does not prescribe a fixed percentage cut (Option C), nor does it link allocations mechanically to GDP growth (Option B); Option D actually describes the opposite of ZBB — approving only increments.

questions.stem: Which of the following items is 'Charged' upon the Consolidated Fund of India and therefore not submitted to vote in Parliament?

options.option_text: Grants-in-aid to State governments under Finance Commission awards
Salaries and allowances payable to the Comptroller and Auditor General
Central sector scheme allocations for infrastructure development
Subsidies on food, fertilizer, and fuel approved in the Union Budget

questions.explanation: Article 148(6) provides that the salary and service conditions of the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) shall be charged upon the Consolidated Fund of India — meaning Parliament discusses but does not vote on it. This protects the CAG's independence. Finance Commission grants, infrastructure scheme outlays, and subsidies are all 'voted' expenditures that require annual parliamentary approval.

questions.stem: The Medium Term Expenditure Framework (MTEF) Statement, mandated under FRBM Rules 2004 (as amended in 2012), is distinct from the Annual Budget primarily because MTEF:

options.option_text: Presents three-year rolling expenditure projections linked to scheme outcomes
Releases funds quarterly only after outcome benchmarks are met by ministries
Imposes a statutory 3% of GDP ceiling on total Central Government expenditure
Requires unspent balances to be returned to the Consolidated Fund within 30 days

questions.explanation: MTEF presents a rolling three-year framework for expenditure projections aligned to the government's policy priorities and scheme outcomes, thereby extending fiscal planning beyond the single-year horizon of the annual budget. Quarterly outcome-linked fund releases (Option B) describe a different performance management mechanism; the 3% GDP cap (Option C) relates to fiscal deficit under FRBM targets, not total expenditure; automatic surrender of unspent funds within 30 days (Option D) is not a feature of MTEF.

questions.stem: The concept of 'Effective Revenue Deficit' (ERD), introduced in Union Budget 2011-12, departs from conventional Revenue Deficit by:

options.option_text: Excluding grants given to States for creation of capital assets from the deficit
Adding off-budget borrowings of Public Sector Enterprises back to the deficit
Subtracting only external debt interest payments from the conventional deficit
Including revenue spending routed through Extra-Budgetary Resources of ministries

questions.explanation: ERD = Revenue Deficit minus Grants for Creation of Capital Assets (GCCA) transferred to States. Since GCCA creates durable productive infrastructure even though it is booked as revenue expenditure, subtracting it from the Revenue Deficit gives a purer picture of consumption-type fiscal imbalance. Off-budget borrowings (Option B) affect the overall fiscal picture but are not the defining feature of ERD; external-debt interest subtraction (Option C) describes no standard budget concept; Extra-Budgetary Resources (Option D) relate to a separate off-balance-sheet borrowing issue.
